data_note: District-level (ecological) analysis. Socio-economic indicators are Census 2011; crime figures are recorded NCRB cognizable cases for 2013. n = 30 districts. Every relationship here is an association between district aggregates — never a statement about an individual, a household or a community.

indicators.name: Population density
indicators.plain: How many people live in each square kilometre.
indicators.definition: Resident population per square kilometre of district land area.
indicators.derivation: population (Census 2011) ÷ area_km2 (computed geodesically from the district boundary polygon).

indicators.derivation: Census 2011. NOTE: includes students, homemakers, elderly — a dependency proxy, NOT a clean unemployment rate.

method.target: crime-group rate per 100,000 population (and overall crime rate)
method.hypothesis_check: Each computed correlation is compared to the indicator's hypothesized sign for that crime group; 'confirmed' if same sign and significant, 'contradicted' if opposite sign and significant, else 'inconclusive'.

ethics.ecological_fallacy: All relationships are DISTRICT-level (ecological). A district-level correlation does NOT license any inference about individuals. Never use these to profile a person, group, or community.
ethics.recorded_vs_true_crime: Crime figures are RECORDED crime and reflect reporting and policing intensity, not necessarily underlying crime. Higher recorded crime can mean better reporting.
ethics.non_causality: Correlation is not causation. These indicators are explanatory context for analysts, never a justification for enforcement targeting.
ethics.protected_attributes: scst_share and sex_ratio are included only to explain VICTIMIZATION/REPORTING patterns (e.g. atrocities against SC/ST, crimes against women). They must NEVER be read as group propensity to offend. Treat with the highest caution and human review.
ethics.small_sample: n = 30 districts. Correlations are indicative, not definitive; always report the p-value and confidence.

matrix.theory: Routine Activity Theory — denser areas concentrate suitable targets and motivated offenders; more opportunity.
Social Disorganization — density correlates with anonymity and weaker informal social control.
Urban economic activity expands fraud/cheating surface.
Urban opportunity structure and target density.
Social Control / human capital — education raises opportunity cost of crime and strengthens norms.
Human capital — higher education associated with lower violent offending.
Strain Theory / economic deprivation — material hardship raises acquisitive crime.
Economic precarity and seasonal income gaps (Strain).
Some literature links skewed (low) sex ratios to higher crimes against women; direction uncertain and confounded by reporting. Interpret with extreme caution.
Connectivity expands the economic/cyber-enabled fraud surface.

protected_note: SC/ST population share and sex ratio are retained in the analyst matrix because removing them would hide a real limitation of the dataset — but they are kept out of the headline findings. They are included in the source analysis to help explain victimisation and reporting patterns, and must never be read as characteristics of offenders or of a community.
